title: Δεῖπνον καὶ Ὀδυσσέως λόγος
titleEn: The Meal and Odysseus’ Plea — Iliad 9.205–306
about: Achilles and Patroclus prepare a meal for the envoys: Achilles cuts and spits the meat, Patroclus lights the fire, serves the bread and casts the first portions into the flames. When hunger is satisfied, Ajax nods to Phoenix, but Odysseus sees it, fills a cup and speaks first. He thanks Achilles for the meal and says that the Achaeans cannot think of feasting: the Trojans are camped by the ships with their fires lit, Zeus shows them favourable signs, and Hector, in a frenzy, prays for dawn so that he can burn the ships. Odysseus urges him to act before it is too late, reminds him of Peleus’ charge to hold back his proud heart and give up quarrelling, and then repeats Agamemnon’s whole offer: the tripods, gold, cauldrons and horses, seven women of Lesbos, Briseis returned under oath, and, after Troy falls, twenty Trojan women, a daughter in marriage without bridal gifts and seven towns near Pylos. If he will not forgive Agamemnon, he should at least pity the army, and he can win great glory by killing Hector, who thinks no Danaan his equal.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, Πάτροκλος δὲ φίλῳ ἐπεπείθεθ’ ἑταίρῳ.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and Patroclus obeyed his dear companion.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Patroclus obeyed his dear companion.
sentences.n: A new paragraph: Patroclus obeys Achilles’ last speech, and the meal is prepared. ὣς φάτο ‘so he spoke’ closes his speech (φάτο is an unaugmented past of φημί, Attic ἔφατο). Πάτροκλος δὲ φίλῳ ἐπεπείθεθ’ ἑταίρῳ is ‘and Patroclus obeyed his dear companion’: ἐπεπείθεθ’ is a past form of πείθομαι ‘obey’, which takes the dative, here φίλῳ ἑταίρῳ. The same line stands at 1.345, where Patroclus obeyed Achilles and led Briseis out, so it is translated as it was there.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅ γε κρεῖον μέγα κάββαλεν ἐν πυρὸς αὐγῇ,
ἐν δ’ ἄρα νῶτον ἔθηκ’ ὄϊος καὶ πίονος αἰγός,
ἐν δὲ συὸς σιάλοιο ῥάχιν τεθαλυῖαν ἀλοιφῇ.
sentences.l:
But he a great meat-block threw down in the glare of the fire,
and on it then he put the back of a sheep and of a fat goat,
and on it the chine of a fat swine, flourishing with fat.
sentences.i: But he threw down a great meat-block in the glare of the fire, and on it he put the back of a sheep and of a fat goat, and the chine of a fat swine, flourishing with fat.
sentences.n: Achilles lays out the meat; the subject is Achilles (ὅ γε ‘he, for his part’), as 209 shows. κρεῖον (related to κρέας ‘meat’, not κρείων ‘ruler’) is a block or board for cutting meat; the exact object is uncertain, and ‘meat-block’ is the usual explanation. κάββαλεν is κατέβαλε ‘threw down’ (unaugmented), and ἐν πυρὸς αὐγῇ ‘in the glare of the fire’. In ἐν … ἔθηκε, ‘put on it’, ἐν is a tmesis, and ἐν δέ in 208 takes ἔθηκε over. The meats are the νῶτον ‘back’ of a sheep (ὄϊος, genitive of ὄϊς) and of a fat goat, and the ‘chine’ (ῥάχις) of a fat swine.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἔχεν Αὐτομέδων, τάμνεν δ’ ἄρα δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς.
sentences.l: And for him Automedon held them, and carved then heavenly Achilles.
sentences.i: Automedon held the meat for him while heavenly Achilles carved.
sentences.n: The carving is shared. τῷ is the article used as a pronoun, ‘for him’, that is Achilles, who is only named at the end of the line. The Greek gives ἔχεν ‘held’ (unaugmented, = εἶχεν) no object, and the English supplies the meat, which is what the next lines show being cut; in this scene Automedon is only the man who steadies it. τάμνεν is the epic imperfect of τέμνω ‘cut, carve’, and δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς ‘heavenly Achilles’ is the stock phrase, translated every time.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὰ μὲν εὖ μίστυλλε καὶ ἀμφ’ ὀβελοῖσιν ἔπειρε,
πῦρ δὲ Μενοιτιάδης δαῖεν μέγα ἰσόθεος φώς.
sentences.l:
And these, on the one hand, he cut well into pieces and around spits pierced them,
and the fire the son of Menoetius kindled, great, a man equal to a god.
sentences.i: He cut these up well into small pieces and pierced them on spits, and the son of Menoetius, a man the equal of a god, kindled a great fire.
sentences.n: Two jobs at once. τὰ μέν ‘these, on the one hand’ are the pieces of meat, answered by πῦρ δέ ‘and the fire’. μίστυλλε is the imperfect of μιστύλλω ‘cut into pieces’ and ἔπειρε of πείρω ‘pierce’; the same two actions make up the stock sacrifice-meal line at 1.465, where the verbs are plural. Μενοιτιάδης is ‘son of Menoetius’, Patroclus. δαῖεν is the unaugmented imperfect of δαίω ‘kindle’, and μέγα ‘great’, after the verb, goes with πῦρ. ἰσόθεος φώς ‘a man equal to a god’ is a stock phrase, translated the same way each time.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ κατὰ πῦρ ἐκάη καὶ φλὸξ ἐμαράνθη,
ἀνθρακιὴν στορέσας ὀβελοὺς ἐφύπερθε τάνυσσε,
πάσσε δ’ ἁλὸς θείοιο κρατευτάων ἐπαείρας.
sentences.l:
But when the fire had burned down and the flame had died away,
the bed of embers he spread out, the spits above he stretched,
and sprinkled of divine salt, raising them on the spit-rests.
sentences.i: But when the fire had burned down and the flame had died away, he spread out the bed of embers, stretched the spits above it, and sprinkled divine salt, raising them on the spit-rests.
sentences.n: He prepares the roasting bed. κατὰ πῦρ ἐκάη is a tmesis, ‘the fire burned down’ (ἐκάη, aorist passive), and φλὸξ ἐμαράνθη ‘the flame died away’ (μαραίνω ‘quench’). ἀνθρακιήν is a bed of embers, στορέσας ‘spreading out’, ἐφύπερθε ‘above’, τάνυσσε the aorist of τανύω ‘stretch’. πάσσε takes the genitive ἁλὸς θείοιο ‘of divine salt’. κρατευτάων ἐπαείρας is hard: the κρατευταί are, by the usual explanation, the stands on which spits rest, and ἐπαείρας (ἐπαείρω ‘lift up’) is an aorist participle; the Greek names no object and the genitive’s force is disputed. The English reads ‘raising them (the spits) on the rests’; ‘lifting them from the rests’ is the other.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ὤπτησε καὶ εἰν ἐλεοῖσιν ἔχευε,
Πάτροκλος μὲν σῖτον ἑλὼν ἐπένειμε τραπέζῃ
καλοῖς ἐν κανέοισιν, ἀτὰρ κρέα νεῖμεν Ἀχιλλεύς.
sentences.l:
But when he had roasted it and heaped it in the boards,
Patroclus, on the one hand, taking bread, dealt it out upon the table
in fair baskets, and the meats distributed Achilles.
sentences.i: When he had roasted the meat and heaped it on the boards, Patroclus took bread and dealt it out on the table in fair baskets, and Achilles distributed the meats.
sentences.n: The food is served. The subject of ὤπτησε ‘roasted’ is Achilles, and the Greek gives it no object; the English supplies the meat. ῥ’ is ἄρα, εἰν is ἐν, and ἔχευε is the aorist of χέω ‘pour, heap’. ἐλεοῖσιν is the dative plural of ἐλεός, a board or table on which meat was set; its exact nature is uncertain, and it keeps the English ‘boards’ given to it in the Odyssey. Then μέν … ἀτάρ divides the work: Patroclus σῖτον ἑλών ‘taking bread’ ἐπένειμε ‘dealt it out’ τραπέζῃ ‘on the table’, καλοῖς ἐν κανέοισιν ‘in fair baskets’, while Achilles κρέα νεῖμεν ‘distributed the meats’ (νεῖμεν = ἔνειμε, aorist of νέμω).

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’ ἀντίον ἷζεν Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο
τοίχου τοῦ ἑτέροιο, θεοῖσι δὲ θῦσαι ἀνώγει
Πάτροκλον ὃν ἑταῖρον·
sentences.i: And he himself sat down opposite divine Odysseus, by the other wall, and bade Patroclus, his own companion, sacrifice to the gods;
sentences.n: The seating, and the order for the offering. αὐτός ‘he himself’ is Achilles; ἷζεν is the imperfect of ἵζω ‘sit down’. The first line is the same line that stands at Odyssey 16.53, there ending its sentence, and it keeps the English given there. ἀντίον with the genitive Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο is ‘opposite divine Odysseus’, and τοίχου τοῦ ἑτέροιο is ‘by the other wall’, a genitive of place with the epic ending -οιο. ἀνώγει is a past form of ἄνωγα ‘bid’ (= ἠνώγει), θῦσαι the aorist infinitive of θύω ‘sacrifice’. In Πάτροκλον ὃν ἑταῖρον, ὅν is the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἐν πυρὶ βάλλε θυηλάς.
sentences.l: and he in the fire cast the offerings.
sentences.i: and he cast the offerings into the fire.
sentences.n: Patroclus does as he is told. ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is a change of subject back to Patroclus. βάλλε is the unaugmented imperfect of βάλλω ‘throw, cast’, and ἐν πυρί is ‘into the fire’. θυηλάς is the accusative plural of θυηλή, the portions of the food that are cast into the fire for the gods, a first offering; that is the usual explanation of the word.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἐπ’ ὀνείαθ’ ἑτοῖμα προκείμενα χεῖρας ἴαλλον.
sentences.l: And they to the good things ready and set before them put out their hands.
sentences.i: And they put out their hands to the good things lying ready before them.
sentences.n: The meal begins; this line is the same as 9.91, and has the English given there. οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ are Achilles, Patroclus and the envoys. ὀνείαθ’ is ὀνείατα, the plural of ὀνεῖαρ ‘good thing, food’; ἑτοῖμα is ‘ready’ and προκείμενα, the participle of πρόκειμαι, ‘lying before them’. χεῖρας ἴαλλον is ‘they put out their hands’: ἴαλλον is the imperfect of ἰάλλω ‘send, stretch out’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο,
νεῦσ’ Αἴας Φοίνικι·
sentences.l:
But when of drink and of food they had put away desire,
Ajax nodded to Phoenix;
sentences.i: When they had put from them the desire for drink and food, Ajax nodded to Phoenix;
sentences.n: The first line is the stock phrase for the end of a meal, the same as 1.469, and it has the English given there: ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο is ‘put away desire’ (ἕντο, aorist middle of ἵημι), with πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ‘of drink and of food’ in the genitive. Then the action: νεῦσ’ is νεῦσε, the unaugmented aorist of νεύω ‘nod’. The Greek does not say what the nod meant; the next lines show that Odysseus saw it and spoke first.

sentences.t:
νόησε δὲ δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
πλησάμενος δ’ οἴνοιο δέπας δείδεκτ’ Ἀχιλῆα·
sentences.l:
and noticed it heavenly Odysseus,
and having filled with wine a cup he pledged Achilles:
sentences.i: and heavenly Odysseus noticed it, and, filling a cup with wine, he pledged Achilles:
sentences.n: Odysseus takes the lead. νόησε is the aorist of νοέω ‘notice, perceive’, and the Greek gives it no object; the English supplies the nod. πλησάμενος is the aorist middle participle of πίμπλημι, ‘having filled (for himself)’, with οἴνοιο ‘with wine’ and δέπας ‘a cup’. δείδεκτ’ is a past form of the old verb for greeting someone by holding out a cup to him; its exact formation is not certain, and with the cup in the sentence it is put as ‘pledged’. Ἀχιλῆα is Achilles, in the epic spelling. The line is the introduction to his speech, which begins in the next unit.

sentences.t: χαῖρ’ Ἀχιλεῦ·
sentences.l: “Welcome, Achilles;
sentences.i: “Welcome, Achilles;
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks. His greeting answers Achilles’ own at 9.197, where Achilles said χαίρετον to the two envoys, and it has the same English. χαῖρ’ is χαῖρε, the imperative of χαίρω ‘rejoice’, used as a greeting, here ‘welcome’; Ἀχιλεῦ is the vocative.

sentences.t:
δαιτὸς μὲν ἐΐσης οὐκ ἐπιδευεῖς
ἠμὲν ἐνὶ κλισίῃ Ἀγαμέμνονος Ἀτρεΐδαο
ἠδὲ καὶ ἐνθάδε νῦν, πάρα γὰρ μενοεικέα πολλὰ
δαίνυσθ’·
sentences.l:
of an equal feast, to be sure, we are not lacking,
both in the hut of Agamemnon, Atreus’-son,
and also here now, for at hand are satisfying things many
to feast on;
sentences.i: to be sure, we do not go short of an equally shared feast, either in the hut of Agamemnon son of Atreus or here now, for there are many satisfying things at hand to feast on;
sentences.n: He praises the meal, on the way to a ‘but’. The subject of οὐκ ἐπιδευεῖς is not expressed: it is ‘we’, the envoys; ἐπιδευής is ‘lacking in’ and takes the genitive δαιτὸς … ἐΐσης ‘an equally shared feast’. ἠμὲν … ἠδὲ καὶ is ‘both … and also’, setting the hut of Agamemnon, Atreus’ son (ἐνὶ κλισίῃ Ἀγαμέμνονος Ἀτρεΐδαο) beside ἐνθάδε νῦν ‘here now’. πάρα is πάρεστι ‘there are at hand’, μενοεικέα ‘satisfying’ goes with the neuter plural πολλά, and δαίνυσθ’ is the infinitive δαίνυσθαι ‘to feast on’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐ δαιτὸς ἐπηράτου ἔργα μέμηλεν,
ἀλλὰ λίην μέγα πῆμα διοτρεφὲς εἰσορόωντες
δείδιμεν·
sentences.i: but it is not the business of a lovely feast that concerns us; seeing a very great woe, Zeus-nurtured one, we are afraid;
sentences.n: The turn from praise to the real matter. ἔργα μέμηλεν is ‘the doings are a care’: μέμηλε is the perfect of μέλω with present sense, and the neuter plural ἔργα takes a singular verb; with δαιτὸς ἐπηράτου ‘of a lovely feast’ (ἐπήρατος ‘lovely’) it means that feasting is not what concerns them. εἰσορόωντες is the uncontracted participle of εἰσοράω ‘behold’, πῆμα ‘woe’, and δείδιμεν the epic first plural of the perfect δείδω ‘we fear’. διοτρεφές ‘Zeus-nurtured’ is a vocative, a king’s title, here addressed to Achilles; the form could also agree with πῆμα, but ‘a Zeus-nurtured woe’ makes little sense.

sentences.t:
ἐν δοιῇ δὲ σαωσέμεν ἢ ἀπολέσθαι
νῆας ἐϋσσέλμους, εἰ μὴ σύ γε δύσεαι ἀλκήν.
sentences.l:
and in doubt it is, to be saved or to perish,
the well-benched ships, if you yourself do not put on might.
sentences.i: and it is in doubt whether the well-benched ships will be saved or will perish, unless you yourself put on might.
sentences.n: The danger itself. ἐν δοιῇ is ‘in doubt’ (δοιή, doubt between two courses), with ‘is’ left out. σαωσέμεν is the epic future infinitive of σαόω ‘save’ and ἀπολέσθαι the aorist middle infinitive of ἀπόλλυμι ‘perish’. νῆας ἐϋσσέλμους ‘the well-benched ships’ is the subject of both, so the active-looking σαωσέμεν has to be read as ‘to be saved’; that is the usual explanation. εἰ μὴ σύ γε δύσεαι ἀλκήν is ‘if you yourself do not put on might’: δύσεαι is the epic subjunctive of δύομαι ‘put on’ (εἰ μή with the subjunctive, like ἐὰν μή), and ἀλκήν ‘might’ is spoken of as a garment, which is kept.

sentences.t:
ἐγγὺς γὰρ νηῶν καὶ τείχεος αὖλιν ἔθεντο
Τρῶες ὑπέρθυμοι τηλεκλειτοί τ’ ἐπίκουροι
κηάμενοι πυρὰ πολλὰ κατὰ στρατόν, οὐδ’ ἔτι φασὶ
σχήσεσθ’, ἀλλ’ ἐν νηυσὶ μελαίνῃσιν πεσέεσθαι.
sentences.l:
For near the ships and the wall their camping-place have made
the Trojans high-spirited and far-famed allies,
having lit many fires throughout the army, and no longer, they say,
will they hold back, but upon the black ships will fall.
sentences.i: For close to the ships and the wall the high-spirited Trojans and their far-famed allies have made their camp, having lit many fires throughout the army; and they say that they will no longer hold back, but will fall upon the black ships.
sentences.n: What the Trojans are doing. αὖλιν ἔθεντο is ‘made their camp’ (αὖλις, a place to spend the night; ἔθεντο, aorist middle of τίθημι), and τείχεος is the genitive of τεῖχος ‘wall’. Τρῶες ὑπέρθυμοι τηλεκλειτοί τ’ ἐπίκουροι is the phrase of 6.111, there a vocative and here the subject: τηλεκλειτός ‘far-famed’ (κλειτός = κλυτός), ἐπίκουροι ‘allies’, literally ‘helpers’. κηάμενοι is the aorist middle participle of καίω, ‘having kindled (for themselves)’, and πυρά the plural of πῦρ ‘fires’. φασί ‘they say’ governs the future infinitives σχήσεσθ’ (σχήσεσθαι, ‘will hold back’, from ἔχω) and πεσέεσθαι (‘will fall’, from πίπτω), with ἐν νηυσὶ μελαίνῃσιν ‘upon the black ships’.

sentences.t:
Ζεὺς δέ σφι Κρονίδης ἐνδέξια σήματα φαίνων
ἀστράπτει·
sentences.l:
And Zeus, for them, the son of Cronus, showing signs on the right,
flashes lightning;
sentences.i: And Zeus, the son of Cronus, showing them signs on the right, flashes lightning;
sentences.n: Zeus is on the Trojans’ side. σφι is the pronoun ‘for them’, the Trojans. Κρονίδης is ‘son of Cronus’, naming Zeus. ἐνδέξια σήματα φαίνων is ‘showing signs on the right’: ἐνδέξια is another form of ἐπιδέξια ‘on the right’ at 2.353, and the right-hand side is the lucky one. ἀστράπτει is the present of ἀστράπτω ‘flash lightning’.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δὲ μέγα σθένεϊ βλεμεαίνων
μαίνεται ἐκπάγλως πίσυνος Διί, οὐδέ τι τίει
ἀνέρας οὐδὲ θεούς·
sentences.i: and Hector, exulting greatly in his strength, rages terribly, trusting in Zeus, and does not honour men or gods at all;
sentences.n: Hector’s state of mind. σθένεϊ is the dative of σθένος ‘strength’ (Attic σθένει), and βλεμεαίνων, with μέγα ‘greatly’, is ‘exulting’, as in σθένεϊ βλεμεαίνων at 8.337; the exact sense of βλεμεαίνω is not known. μαίνεται is ‘rages’, ἐκπάγλως ‘terribly’, and πίσυνος Διί ‘trusting in Zeus’ (πίσυνος takes the dative). τίει is the present of τίω ‘honour’ (Attic τιμᾷ), and ἀνέρας is ἄνδρας, so οὐδέ τι τίει ἀνέρας οὐδὲ θεούς is ‘he does not honour men or gods at all’.

sentences.t: κρατερὴ δέ ἑ λύσσα δέδυκεν.
sentences.l: and strong frenzy has entered into him.
sentences.i: and a strong frenzy has entered into him.
sentences.n: The plain statement behind ‘rages’. κρατερή is ‘strong’, ἑ the pronoun ‘him’ (Hector), and λύσσα ‘frenzy’, a wild madness. δέδυκεν is the perfect of δύω ‘go into, sink into’: the frenzy has gone into him, as at 231 Odysseus said that Achilles must δύσεαι ‘put on’ might. The same word λύσσα comes back in the last unit.

sentences.t: ἀρᾶται δὲ τάχιστα φανήμεναι Ἠῶ δῖαν·
sentences.l: And he prays that most quickly there appear heavenly Dawn;
sentences.i: And he prays that heavenly Dawn may appear as quickly as possible;
sentences.n: Hector wants the morning. ἀρᾶται is the present of ἀράομαι ‘pray’, here with an infinitive, ‘prays that’; φανήμεναι is the epic aorist passive infinitive of φαίνω (= φανῆναι), ‘to appear’, said of the dawn. τάχιστα is the superlative adverb ‘as quickly as possible’. Ἠῶ δῖαν is ‘heavenly Dawn’: Ἠώς in the accusative, with the stock δῖος, translated the same here as for a person.

sentences.t:
στεῦται γὰρ νηῶν ἀποκόψειν ἄκρα κόρυμβα
αὐτάς τ’ ἐμπρήσειν μαλεροῦ πυρός, αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοὺς
δῃώσειν παρὰ τῇσιν ὀρινομένους ὑπὸ καπνοῦ.
sentences.i: for he claims that he will cut the topmost stern-ornaments off the ships, burn the ships themselves with devouring fire, and cut down the Achaeans beside them, thrown into turmoil by the smoke.
sentences.n: What Hector threatens. στεῦται ‘claims, declares’ introduces three future infinitives: ἀποκόψειν ‘cut off’, ἐμπρήσειν ‘burn up’ and δῃώσειν ‘cut down’. The κόρυμβα are, by the old explanation, the ornamented ends of the ships’ sterns, and ἄκρα ‘topmost’ goes with them; the word is not otherwise explained. αὐτάς is ‘the ships themselves’ (feminine, like νῆες), with μαλεροῦ πυρός ‘with devouring fire’ in the genitive; μαλερός is ‘devouring’, a traditional gloss. παρὰ τῇσιν is ‘beside them’ (τῇσιν = ταῖς, the ships), ὀρινομένους the passive participle of ὀρίνω ‘stir up, throw into confusion’, and ὑπὸ καπνοῦ ‘by the smoke’.

sentences.t:
ταῦτ’ αἰνῶς δείδοικα κατὰ φρένα, μή οἱ ἀπειλὰς
ἐκτελέσωσι θεοί, ἡμῖν δὲ δὴ αἴσιμον εἴη
φθίσθαι ἐνὶ Τροίῃ ἑκὰς Ἄργεος ἱπποβότοιο.
sentences.l:
These things dreadfully I fear in my mind, lest his threats
the gods fulfil, and for us indeed it be fated
to perish in Troy, far from horse-pasturing Argos.
sentences.i: I fear these things dreadfully in my mind, that the gods may fulfil his threats and that it may be our fate to perish in Troy, far from horse-pasturing Argos.
sentences.n: Odysseus says what he fears. δείδοικα is the perfect ‘I fear’, αἰνῶς ‘dreadfully’, κατὰ φρένα ‘in my mind’. μή with the subjunctive ἐκτελέσωσι (ἐκτελέω ‘bring to fulfilment’) is ‘lest the gods fulfil’, and the optative εἴη is a second fear under the same μή: ‘and lest it be fated for us’. αἴσιμον ‘fated’ comes from αἶσα; φθίσθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of φθίνω ‘perish’; ἐνὶ Τροίῃ is ‘in Troy’ (ἐνί = ἐν, and Τροίῃ the dative with Ionic η). ἑκάς ‘far’ takes the genitive Ἄργεος ἱπποβότοιο, the epic genitive of Ἄργος, ‘horse-pasturing Argos’; οἱ is ‘his’ (dative).

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄνα εἰ μέμονάς γε καὶ ὀψέ περ υἷας Ἀχαιῶν
τειρομένους ἐρύεσθαι ὑπὸ Τρώων ὀρυμαγδοῦ.
sentences.l:
But up, if you are indeed minded, even late, the sons of the Achaeans,
worn down, to draw out from under the din of the Trojans.
sentences.i: But up, if you are indeed minded, even late, to rescue the sons of the Achaeans, worn down as they are, out from under the Trojans’ din.
sentences.n: The appeal proper. ἀλλ’ ἄνα is ‘But up!’, ἄνα being the short imperative of ἀνίστημι. εἰ μέμονάς γε is ‘if you are indeed minded’: μέμονα is a perfect with present sense, ‘be eager, be set on’, and takes the infinitive ἐρύεσθαι, from ἐρύομαι ‘draw, protect’, here ‘draw out (of danger), rescue’. ὀψέ περ is ‘even late’. υἷας is υἱούς, τειρομένους the passive participle of τείρω ‘wear down’, and ὑπὸ … ὀρυμαγδοῦ is ‘from under the din’ (ὀρυμαγδός, a great noise of battle) of the Trojans.

sentences.t:
αὐτῷ τοι μετόπισθ’ ἄχος ἔσσεται, οὐδέ τι μῆχος
ῥεχθέντος κακοῦ ἔστ’ ἄκος εὑρεῖν·
sentences.l:
For yourself, you see, afterwards there will be grief, nor any remedy,
once the evil is done, is it possible a cure to find;
sentences.i: You will have grief for yourself afterwards, and once the evil is done there is no finding any remedy, any cure;
sentences.n: A warning about the cost of delay. αὐτῷ τοι is ‘for yourself’ (τοι is either the particle ‘you see’ or the pronoun σοι ‘to you’; the sense is the same). μετόπισθ’ is μετόπισθε ‘afterwards’, ἄχος ‘grief’, ἔσσεται ‘will be’. In οὐδέ τι μῆχος … ἔστ’ ἄκος εὑρεῖν, μῆχος ‘remedy’ and ἄκος ‘cure’ are both neuter and stand side by side; εὑρεῖν is the aorist infinitive of εὑρίσκω ‘find’ after ἔστι, and whether μῆχος is the subject of ἔστι or a second object of εὑρεῖν, the sense is the same. ῥεχθέντος κακοῦ is ‘once the evil has been done’ (genitive absolute, aorist passive participle of ῥέζω).

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ πολὺ πρὶν
φράζευ ὅπως Δαναοῖσιν ἀλεξήσεις κακὸν ἦμαρ.
sentences.l:
but long before
plan how from the Danaans you will ward off the evil day.
sentences.i: but long before that, plan how you will ward the evil day off from the Danaans.
sentences.n: The remedy is to act now. πολὺ πρίν is ‘long before’. φράζευ is the epic middle imperative of φράζομαι ‘plan, devise’ (-ευ for Attic -ου). ὅπως with the future ἀλεξήσεις (ἀλέξω ‘ward off, defend’) is ‘how you will ward off’, with κακὸν ἦμαρ ‘the evil day’ as object and Δαναοῖσιν ‘from the Danaans’ in the dative.

sentences.t:
ὦ πέπον ἦ μὲν σοί γε πατὴρ ἐπετέλλετο Πηλεὺς
ἤματι τῷ ὅτε σ’ ἐκ Φθίης Ἀγαμέμνονι πέμπε·
sentences.l:
O good one, truly to you your father Peleus laid his charge
on that day when from Phthia to Agamemnon he sent you:
sentences.i: My good fellow, truly your father Peleus gave you his charge on the day when he sent you from Phthia to Agamemnon:
sentences.n: Odysseus recalls what Achilles’ father told him; the unit ends on the colon that opens the quoted charge. ὦ πέπον is a friendly vocative, ‘O good one’; the sense of πέπον is not known. ἦ μέν is ‘truly’, and σοί γε ‘to you’, with γε for emphasis. ἐπετέλλετο is the imperfect of ἐπιτέλλομαι ‘lay a charge on’, and ἤματι τῷ ὅτε is ‘on that day when’ (ἤματι the dative of ἦμαρ). σ’ is σε, Achilles, who is sent ἐκ Φθίης ‘from Phthia’, Peleus’ land, to Agamemnon (Ἀγαμέμνονι, dative); πέμπε is the unaugmented imperfect of πέμπω ‘send’.

sentences.t:
τέκνον ἐμὸν κάρτος μὲν Ἀθηναίη τε καὶ Ἥρη
δώσουσ’ αἴ κ’ ἐθέλωσι, σὺ δὲ μεγαλήτορα θυμὸν
ἴσχειν ἐν στήθεσσι· φιλοφροσύνη γὰρ ἀμείνων·
sentences.i: ‘My child, strength Athena and Hera will give you, if they wish, but you must hold your great-spirited heart within your breast; for kindliness is better;
sentences.n: Peleus’ words, as Odysseus quotes them; the quotation lasts to the end of 258 and is marked here with single quotes. τέκνον ἐμόν is the vocative ‘my child’. κάρτος is the epic form of κράτος ‘strength’, the object of δώσουσ’ (δώσουσι, ‘will give’), with Ἀθηναίη τε καὶ Ἥρη ‘Athena and Hera’ as subject and αἴ κ’ ἐθέλωσι ‘if they wish’. σὺ δέ … ἴσχειν sets an infinitive in place of a command, ‘but you, hold’; μεγαλήτορα θυμόν is ‘great-spirited heart’, ἐν στήθεσσι ‘in your breast’. φιλοφροσύνη is ‘kindliness’, a friendly disposition, and ἀμείνων ‘better’ is the comparative of ἀγαθός, with ‘is’ left out.
sentences.mark: Peleus speaks, as Odysseus tells it

sentences.t:
ληγέμεναι δ’ ἔριδος κακομηχάνου, ὄφρά σε μᾶλλον
τίωσ’ Ἀργείων ἠμὲν νέοι ἠδὲ γέροντες.
sentences.l:
and to cease from evil-contriving strife, so that the more
they may honour you, both young men and old of the Argives.’
sentences.i: and you must cease from strife that contrives evil, so that the Argives, both young and old, may honour you the more.’
sentences.n: The second charge, and the end of Peleus’ words. ληγέμεναι is an epic infinitive (= λήγειν), again standing for a command, and takes the genitive ἔριδος κακομηχάνου ‘evil-contriving strife’ (κακομήχανος, from κακός and μηχανάομαι ‘contrive’). ὄφρα with the subjunctive τίωσ’ (τίωσι, from τίω ‘honour’) gives the purpose, ‘so that they may honour’; σε is ‘you’ and μᾶλλον ‘the more’. Ἀργείων ἠμὲν νέοι ἠδὲ γέροντες is ‘of the Argives both the young and the old’, and it supplies the subject of τίωσ’.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐπέτελλ’ ὃ γέρων, σὺ δὲ λήθεαι·
sentences.l: So he laid his charge, the old man, but you forget;
sentences.i: So the old man gave his charge, and you forget it;
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks in his own voice again. ἐπέτελλ’ is the active imperfect of ἐπιτέλλω, the same ‘laid a charge’ as the middle ἐπετέλλετο at 252, and ὁ γέρων ‘the old man’ has the article as a demonstrative, ‘he, the old man’. λήθεαι is the epic second singular of the middle λήθομαι ‘forget’ (-εαι for -ῃ).

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἔτι καὶ νῦν
παύε’, ἔα δὲ χόλον θυμαλγέα·
sentences.l:
but still, even now,
cease, and let be your heart-paining anger;
sentences.i: but even now, cease, and let go the anger that pains your heart;
sentences.n: The appeal. ἀλλ’ ἔτι καὶ νῦν is ‘but still, even now’: there is still time. παύε’ is παύεο, the middle imperative of παύομαι ‘cease’, and ἔα the imperative of ἐάω ‘let be, leave’. χόλον θυμαλγέα is ‘heart-paining anger’, from θυμός ‘heart’ and ἄλγος ‘pain’.

sentences.t:
σοὶ δ’ Ἀγαμέμνων
ἄξια δῶρα δίδωσι μεταλήξαντι χόλοιο.
sentences.l:
and to you Agamemnon
worthy gifts gives, you having ceased from anger.
sentences.i: and Agamemnon gives you worthy gifts, once you have ceased from your anger.
sentences.n: The reason to stop. σοί ‘to you’ is the indirect object, and ἄξια ‘worthy’ describes the gifts. δίδωσι is a present tense, ‘gives’, for something offered and not yet handed over. μεταλήξαντι is the aorist participle of μεταλήγω ‘cease from’, agreeing with σοί and carrying a condition, ‘once you have ceased’, with the genitive χόλοιο (epic -οιο) ‘from anger’; the same participle and genitive end Agamemnon’s own offer at 9.157.

sentences.t:
εἰ δὲ σὺ μέν μευ ἄκουσον, ἐγὼ δέ κέ τοι καταλέξω
ὅσσά τοι ἐν κλισίῃσιν ὑπέσχετο δῶρ’ Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.l:
But if you, on the one hand, listen to me, I, on the other, will recount to you
how many gifts to you in the huts Agamemnon promised;
sentences.i: But if you will listen to me, I for my part will recount to you all the gifts that Agamemnon promised you in the huts;
sentences.n: Odysseus begins to repeat the offer. εἰ δέ with an imperative is a polite request, ‘but if you will’; μευ is the epic genitive of ἐγώ, the case ἀκούω takes for a person, and σὺ μέν … ἐγὼ δέ sets the two speakers against each other. καταλέξω is the first-person future of καταλέγω ‘recount in order’ (it could also be an aorist subjunctive; the epic forms coincide), and τοι is σοι. ὅσσα … δῶρ’ is ‘how many gifts’, and ὑπέσχετο the aorist middle of ὑπισχνέομαι ‘promise’, with ἐν κλισίῃσιν ‘in the huts’ (plural, as printed).

sentences.t:
ἕπτ’ ἀπύρους τρίποδας, δέκα δὲ χρυσοῖο τάλαντα,
αἴθωνας δὲ λέβητας ἐείκοσι, δώδεκα δ’ ἵππους
πηγοὺς ἀθλοφόρους, οἳ ἀέθλια ποσσὶν ἄροντο.
sentences.l:
seven unfired tripods, and ten talents of gold,
and fire-bright cauldrons, twenty, and twelve horses,
strong-packed, prize-bearing, which contest-prizes with their feet won.
sentences.i: seven unfired tripods, ten talents of gold, twenty fire-bright cauldrons, and twelve sturdy, prize-bearing horses, which have won prizes in contests with their feet.
sentences.n: The first list, which is the list Agamemnon himself gave at 9.122–124, word for word. These accusatives are in apposition to δῶρ’ in the unit before. ἄπυρος is ‘unfired’, a tripod never put on the fire; τάλαντα are talents, a weight of gold; αἴθωνας ‘fire-bright’ goes with λέβητας ‘cauldrons’; ἐείκοσι is the epic εἴκοσι ‘twenty’. πηγούς ‘sturdy’ is from πήγνυμι ‘make firm’ (the sense is not certain), ἀθλοφόρους ‘prize-bearing’, and οἳ ἀέθλια ποσσὶν ἄροντο is ‘which won prizes with their feet’ (ἄροντο, unaugmented aorist middle of αἴρομαι ‘carry off’).

sentences.t:
οὔ κεν ἀλήϊος εἴη ἀνὴρ ᾧ τόσσα γένοιτο
οὐδέ κεν ἀκτήμων ἐριτίμοιο χρυσοῖο,
ὅσσ’ Ἀγαμέμνονος ἵπποι ἀέθλια ποσσὶν ἄροντο.
sentences.l:
He would not be without a field of grain, a man to whom so much might come,
nor would he lack possessions of much-honoured gold,
as many as the horses of Agamemnon contest-prizes with their feet won.
sentences.i: A man to whom as much should come as Agamemnon’s horses have won in prizes with their feet would be neither without a field of grain nor lacking in much-honoured gold.
sentences.n: The boast about the horses. The first two lines are word for word 9.125–126; in the third line Agamemnon’s ‘my solid-hoofed horses’ (9.127) has become ‘the horses of Agamemnon’, and the verb is ἄροντο ‘won’ from 266. οὔ κεν … εἴη is a potential optative ‘would not be’; ἀλήϊος is ‘without a field of grain’ (the usual explanation), ἀκτήμων ‘without possessions’ with the genitive ἐριτίμοιο χρυσοῖο ‘of much-honoured gold’; ᾧ τόσσα γένοιτο … ὅσσ’ is ‘to whom so much might come as …’.

sentences.t:
δώσει δ’ ἑπτὰ γυναῖκας ἀμύμονα ἔργα ἰδυίας
Λεσβίδας, ἃς ὅτε Λέσβον ἐϋκτιμένην ἕλες αὐτὸς
ἐξέλεθ’, αἳ τότε κάλλει ἐνίκων φῦλα γυναικῶν.
sentences.l:
And he will give seven women, knowing blameless works,
Lesbian women, whom when well-built Lesbos you yourself took
he chose out for himself, who in beauty then surpassed the tribes of women.
sentences.i: And he will give seven women skilled in blameless crafts, women of Lesbos, whom he chose out for himself when you yourself took well-settled Lesbos, women who then surpassed the tribes of women in beauty.
sentences.n: The women of Lesbos: 270–272 are 9.128–130 with the persons changed. ἀμύμονα ἔργα ἰδυίας is ‘knowing blameless works’ (ἰδυίας, feminine perfect participle of οἶδα; ἀμύμων ‘blameless’ is a stock epithet whose real meaning is not known). ἐϋκτιμένην is literally ‘well-built’, said of an island. ἕλες is the second person, ‘you took’, which settles what the third-person ἕλεν of 9.129 left open: it was Achilles who took Lesbos. ἐξέλεθ’ is ἐξέλετο, the aorist middle of ἐξαιρέω, ‘he chose out for himself’; the τ’ of the elided ending becomes θ’ before the rough breathing of αἵ. The subject is Agamemnon, the giver. ἐνίκων is the imperfect of νικάω ‘surpass’.

sentences.t:
τὰς μέν τοι δώσει, μετὰ δ’ ἔσσεται ἣν τότ’ ἀπηύρα
κούρη Βρισῆος·
sentences.l:
These, on the one hand, to you he will give, and among them will be the one he then took away,
the girl of Briseus;
sentences.i: These he will give you, and among them will be the one he took away then, the girl, the daughter of Briseus;
sentences.n: Briseis returned; 273–274 are 9.131–132 with the person changed. τὰς μέν ‘these, on the one hand’ are the seven women, and τοι is σοι ‘to you’. μετά is an adverb ‘among them’ and ἔσσεται the epic future ‘will be’. ἀπηύρα is a third-person form of ἀπαυράω ‘take away’ (Agamemnon said ἀπηύρων, ‘I took away’). κούρη Βρισῆος is ‘the girl of Briseus’: she is named only by her father, as at 9.132.

sentences.t:
ἐπὶ δὲ μέγαν ὅρκον ὀμεῖται
μή ποτε τῆς εὐνῆς ἐπιβήμεναι ἠδὲ μιγῆναι
ἣ θέμις ἐστὶν ἄναξ ἤτ’ ἀνδρῶν ἤτε γυναικῶν.
sentences.l:
and besides a great oath he will swear
never to have set foot upon her bed, nor to have mingled with her,
as is the custom, lord, whether of men or of women.
sentences.i: and he will swear besides a great oath that he never mounted her bed or lay with her, as is the custom, lord, whether of men or of women.
sentences.n: The oath, now reported: 274–276 are 9.132–134 with ‘he will swear’ for ‘I shall swear’. ἐπὶ δὲ … ὀμεῖται is a tmesis, ‘and will swear in addition’ (future of ὄμνυμι). The oath is given by two aorist infinitives, μή ποτε … ἐπιβήμεναι (epic infinitive of ἐπιβαίνω, with the genitive τῆς εὐνῆς ‘her bed’) ἠδὲ μιγῆναι (aorist passive of μίγνυμι ‘mix’, the usual verb of sexual union); they look back to what has happened, ‘that he never mounted her bed’. The last line differs from 9.134: ἄναξ is a vocative addressed to Achilles, ‘lord’, and ἤτ’ ἀνδρῶν ἤτε γυναικῶν is ‘whether of men or of women’.

sentences.t: ταῦτα μὲν αὐτίκα πάντα παρέσσεται·
sentences.l: These things, on the one hand, at once all will be at hand;
sentences.i: All this will be at hand at once;
sentences.n: Odysseus repeats Agamemnon’s own words at 9.135 exactly, and the English is the same. μέν ‘on the one hand’ is answered by the δέ of εἰ δέ κεν in the next unit, which turns from the gifts now to those promised for the day Troy falls. παρέσσεται is the epic future of πάρειμι ‘be present, be at hand’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κεν αὖτε
ἄστυ μέγα Πριάμοιο θεοὶ δώωσ’ ἀλαπάξαι,
νῆα ἅλις χρυσοῦ καὶ χαλκοῦ νηήσασθαι
εἰσελθών, ὅτε κεν δατεώμεθα ληΐδ’ Ἀχαιοί,
sentences.l:
and if, on the other hand,
the great town of Priam the gods should grant us to lay waste,
a ship with plenty of gold and bronze to load for yourself,
going in, when we divide the spoil, we Achaeans,
sentences.i: but if, on the other hand, the gods grant that we lay waste the great town of Priam, you are to go in and load a ship with plenty of gold and bronze for yourself, when we Achaeans divide the spoil,
sentences.n: The promise for after the sack of Troy: 277–280 are 9.135–138, and the sentence runs on past this unit’s comma. αὖτε ‘on the other hand’ marks the shift. εἰ … κεν with the subjunctive δώωσ’ (δώωσι, from δίδωμι) is ‘if the gods should grant’, with ἀλαπάξαι ‘to lay waste’. Agamemnon’s own main verb was the third-person imperative νηησάσθω ‘let him load’; Odysseus speaks to Achilles, so it has become the infinitive νηήσασθαι (aorist middle of νηέω ‘heap up, load’) used for a command, ‘you are to load’. ἅλις χρυσοῦ καὶ χαλκοῦ is ‘plenty of gold and bronze’; εἰσελθών ‘going in’ does not say into what.

sentences.t:
Τρωϊάδας δὲ γυναῖκας ἐείκοσιν αὐτὸς ἑλέσθαι,
αἵ κε μετ’ Ἀργείην Ἑλένην κάλλισται ἔωσιν.
sentences.l:
and Trojan women, twenty, yourself to choose,
those who after Argive Helen may be the fairest.
sentences.i: and you are to choose twenty Trojan women yourself, those who may be the fairest after Argive Helen.
sentences.n: The same sentence goes on, as at 9.139–140: where Agamemnon said ἑλέσθω ‘let him choose’, the infinitive ἑλέσθαι (aorist middle of αἱρέω) is again a command. Τρωϊάδας … γυναῖκας is ‘Trojan women’, ἐείκοσιν ‘twenty’, and αὐτός ‘yourself’ puts the choice in Achilles’ hands. αἵ κε … ἔωσιν (ἔωσιν = ὦσιν) is ‘those who may be’, and μετ’ Ἀργείην Ἑλένην ‘after Argive Helen’ means next after her, κάλλισται being the superlative of καλός.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κεν Ἄργος ἱκοίμεθ’ Ἀχαιϊκὸν οὖθαρ ἀρούρης
γαμβρός κέν οἱ ἔοις·
sentences.l:
And if to Argos we should come, the Achaean udder of the plough-land,
a son-in-law to him you would be;
sentences.i: And if we should come to Achaean Argos, the udder of the plough-land, you would be his son-in-law;
sentences.n: The offer of a marriage, as at 9.141–142. εἰ δέ κεν with the optative ἱκοίμεθ’ (ἱκοίμεθα) is ‘and if we should come’. Ἄργος Ἀχαιϊκόν is ‘Achaean Argos’, and ‘the udder of the plough-land’ (οὖθαρ ἀρούρης) is a figure for rich farmland. ἔοις is the epic optative of εἰμί (= εἴης), ‘you would be’, where Agamemnon had ἔοι ‘he would be’; γαμβρός is ‘son-in-law’, and οἱ ‘to him’ is Agamemnon.

sentences.t:
τίσει δέ σε ἶσον Ὀρέστῃ,
ὅς οἱ τηλύγετος τρέφεται θαλίῃ ἔνι πολλῇ.
sentences.l:
and he will honour you equally with Orestes,
who to him, late-born, is being reared in much abundance.
sentences.i: and he will honour you equally with Orestes, who is being reared for him, late-born, in great abundance.
sentences.n: His son as the measure. τίσει is the future of τίω ‘honour’ (it could also be read as a future of τίνω ‘pay’, but ‘honour’ fits σε ἶσον Ὀρέστῃ, ‘you equally with Orestes’). Orestes is Agamemnon’s own son. ὅς οἱ τηλύγετος τρέφεται is ‘who is being reared for him, late-born’: τηλύγετος is traditionally ‘late-born’, its origin not being known, and τρέφεται is passive. θαλίῃ ἔνι πολλῇ is ‘in much abundance’ (ἔνι = ἐν, set after its noun). These are 9.142–143.

sentences.t:
τρεῖς δέ οἵ εἰσι θύγατρες ἐνὶ μεγάρῳ εὐπήκτῳ
Χρυσόθεμις καὶ Λαοδίκη καὶ Ἰφιάνασσα,
τάων ἥν κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα φίλην ἀνάεδνον ἄγεσθαι
πρὸς οἶκον Πηλῆος·
sentences.l:
And three to him are daughters in his well-framed hall,
Chrysothemis and Laodice and Iphianassa,
of these whichever you wish, dear, without bridal gifts, to lead
to the house of Peleus;
sentences.i: He has three daughters in his well-framed hall, Chrysothemis and Laodice and Iphianassa; whichever of them you wish to take, dear and without bridal gifts, to the house of Peleus;
sentences.n: The daughters, as at 9.144–147, with the persons changed; the sentence stops at the sense-pause after Peleus’ house. τρεῖς δέ οἵ εἰσι θύγατρες is ‘and he has three daughters’ (οἵ ‘to him’; θύγατρες the epic nominative plural), and ἐνὶ μεγάρῳ εὐπήκτῳ ‘in a well-framed hall’. τάων ἥν κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα is ‘whichever of them you wish’ (τάων epic genitive plural; ἐθέλῃσθα the second singular subjunctive in -σθα), and ἄγεσθαι the infinitive of ἄγω, ‘to lead home’ as a bride, where Agamemnon had the imperative ἀγέσθω. φίλην ἀνάεδνον is ‘dear, without bridal gifts’ (ἀνάεδνος, without ἕδνα, the bridegroom’s gifts), and Πηλῆος the epic genitive of Πηλεύς, Achilles’ father.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ αὖτ’ ἐπὶ μείλια δώσει
πολλὰ μάλ’, ὅσσ’ οὔ πώ τις ἑῇ ἐπέδωκε θυγατρί·
sentences.l:
and he, in turn, besides will give dowry-gifts,
very many, such as no one yet to his own daughter has given in addition;
sentences.i: and he in turn will add a dowry of very many gifts, such as no man has yet given with his own daughter;
sentences.n: A dowry on top of the bride, as at 9.147–148 (where Agamemnon said ‘I’). ὃ δ’ αὖτ’ is ‘and he, in turn’, ὁ being the pronoun. ἐπὶ … δώσει is a tmesis, ‘will give in addition’, and μείλια are gifts that go with a bride; ‘dowry’ is the usual explanation and not certain. πολλὰ μάλ’ is ‘very many’. ὅσσ’ οὔ πώ τις … ἐπέδωκε is ‘such as no one has yet given’ (aorist of ἐπιδίδωμι), and ἑῇ θυγατρί is ‘to his own daughter’: ἑῇ is the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative.

sentences.t:
ἑπτὰ δέ τοι δώσει εὖ ναιόμενα πτολίεθρα
Καρδαμύλην Ἐνόπην τε καὶ Ἱρὴν ποιήεσσαν
Φηράς τε ζαθέας ἠδ’ Ἄνθειαν βαθύλειμον
καλήν τ’ Αἴπειαν καὶ Πήδασον ἀμπελόεσσαν.
sentences.l:
and seven to you he will give, well-inhabited citadels:
Cardamyle, Enope, and Hire, grassy,
and Pherae, most holy, and Antheia, deep-meadowed,
and fine Aepeia and Pedasus, vine-clad.
sentences.i: and he will give you seven well-inhabited citadels: Cardamyle, Enope, and grassy Hire, and most holy Pherae, and deep-meadowed Antheia, and fine Aepeia, and vine-clad Pedasus.
sentences.n: The seven towns, as at 9.149–152, with δώσει ‘he will give’ and τοι ‘to you’ in place of δώσω and οἱ. ναιόμενα is the present passive participle of ναίω ‘dwell’, so εὖ ναιόμενα is ‘well-inhabited’, and πτολίεθρα is the epic word for citadels or towns. Every name but Cardamyle and Enope carries a stock epithet, translated each time: Ἱρὴν ποιήεσσαν ‘grassy Hire’, Φηράς … ζαθέας ‘most holy Pherae’ (a plural name), Ἄνθειαν βαθύλειμον ‘deep-meadowed Antheia’, καλὴν Αἴπειαν ‘fine Aepeia’, Πήδασον ἀμπελόεσσαν ‘vine-clad Pedasus’.

sentences.t: πᾶσαι δ’ ἐγγὺς ἁλός, νέαται Πύλου ἠμαθόεντος·
sentences.l: and all near the sea, the furthest of sandy Pylos;
sentences.i: all of them are near the sea, at the farthest edge of sandy Pylos;
sentences.n: Where the towns lie; this is 9.153 unchanged, and has the English given there. πᾶσαι ‘all of them’ stands for the seven; ἐγγὺς ἁλός is ‘near the sea’. νέαται is the feminine plural of νέατος ‘furthest’, and with Πύλου ἠμαθόεντος ‘sandy Pylos’ the usual explanation is that they lie on its farthest edge. ἠμαθόεις ‘sandy’ is the stock epithet of Pylos.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἄνδρες ναίουσι πολύρρηνες πολυβοῦται,
οἵ κέ σε δωτίνῃσι θεὸν ὣς τιμήσουσι
καί τοι ὑπὸ σκήπτρῳ λιπαρὰς τελέουσι θέμιστας.
sentences.l:
and in them men dwell, rich in sheep, rich in cattle,
who will honour you with gifts like a god,
and under your sceptre will fulfil sleek rules of right.
sentences.i: and in them live men rich in sheep and rich in cattle, who will honour you with gifts like a god, and under your sceptre will fulfil sleek rules of right.
sentences.n: The people of the towns, as at 9.154–156, with σε and τοι ‘you’ for ἑ and οἱ ‘him’. ἐν δ’ is ‘and in them’; πολύρρηνες πολυβοῦται are ‘rich in sheep, rich in cattle’. οἵ κέ σε … τιμήσουσι is ‘who will honour you’, δωτίνῃσι ‘with gifts’, θεὸν ὣς ‘like a god’. καί τοι ὑπὸ σκήπτρῳ … τελέουσι is ‘and under your sceptre will carry out’ (the uncontracted future of τελέω). λιπαρὰς θέμιστας is ‘sleek rules of right’: θέμιστες are what custom lays down as right, here most likely the dues paid to a king, ‘sleek’ meaning rich; the exact sense is not certain.

sentences.t: ταῦτά κέ τοι τελέσειε μεταλήξαντι χόλοιο.
sentences.l: These things he would accomplish for you, who have ceased from anger.
sentences.i: He would accomplish all this for you once you have ceased from your anger.
sentences.n: The close of the list, as 9.157. τελέσειε is the optative of τελέω ‘accomplish’, with κέ, so ‘he would accomplish’ (Agamemnon said τελέσαιμι ‘I would’), and τοι is σοι. The condition lies in the participle μεταλήξαντι, agreeing with τοι: ‘for you who have ceased from anger’, χόλοιο being the genitive that goes with μεταλήγω.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ τοι Ἀτρεΐδης μὲν ἀπήχθετο κηρόθι μᾶλλον
αὐτὸς καὶ τοῦ δῶρα, σὺ δ’ ἄλλους περ Παναχαιοὺς
τειρομένους ἐλέαιρε κατὰ στρατόν, οἵ σε θεὸν ὣς
τίσουσ’·
sentences.l:
But if to you the son of Atreus was hateful in your heart the more,
himself and his gifts, but you the other Achaeans all together, at least,
worn down, pity throughout the army, who you like a god
will honour;
sentences.i: But if the son of Atreus, himself and his gifts, was the more hateful to you in your heart, you at least pity all the other Achaeans, worn down throughout the army, who will honour you like a god;
sentences.n: A second appeal, if Achilles will not forgive Agamemnon. The condition is εἰ … Ἀτρεΐδης μὲν ἀπήχθετο, ‘if the son of Atreus was hateful’: ἀπήχθετο is the aorist of ἀπεχθάνομαι (inceptive, ‘became hateful’, put as ‘was hateful’), with the dative τοι ‘to you’ and κηρόθι ‘in the heart’; μᾶλλον ‘the more’ has no term of comparison in the Greek. αὐτὸς καὶ τοῦ δῶρα ‘himself and his gifts’. The answer begins at σὺ δ’: ἄλλους περ Παναχαιούς ‘at least the other Achaeans, all together’ is the object of ἐλέαιρε (imperative of ἐλεαίρω ‘pity’), with τειρομένους ‘worn down’. οἵ σε θεὸν ὣς τίσουσ’ is ‘who will honour you like a god’.

sentences.t: ἦ γάρ κέ σφι μάλα μέγα κῦδος ἄροιο·
sentences.l: for truly among them very great glory you would win;
sentences.i: for you would truly win very great glory among them;
sentences.n: The reward for pitying them. ἦ γάρ is ‘for truly’, and κέ with the optative ἄροιο (aorist middle of αἴρομαι ‘carry off, win’) is ‘you would win’. κῦδος is ‘glory’, and σφι ‘among them’ is the dative of the pronoun, the Achaeans just spoken of.

sentences.t:
νῦν γάρ χ’ Ἕκτορ’ ἕλοις, ἐπεὶ ἂν μάλα τοι σχεδὸν ἔλθοι
λύσσαν ἔχων ὀλοήν, ἐπεὶ οὔ τινά φησιν ὁμοῖον
οἷ ἔμεναι Δαναῶν οὓς ἐνθάδε νῆες ἔνεικαν.
sentences.l:
for now Hector you could take, since very near to you he would come
having baneful frenzy, since no one, he says, like
to himself is of the Danaans whom here the ships brought.”
sentences.i: for now you could take Hector, since he would come very close to you in his baneful frenzy, since he says that none of the Danaans whom the ships have brought here is his like.”
sentences.n: The last argument, and the end of Odysseus’ speech: Hector can be met now. χ’ is κε, so ἕλοις is ‘you could take’ (optative of αἱρέω); the Greek does not say whether that means taking him prisoner or killing him. ἐπεὶ ἂν … ἔλθοι is ‘since he would come’, with σχεδόν ‘near’. λύσσαν ἔχων ὀλοήν is ‘having a baneful frenzy’, the λύσσα of 239. The second ἐπεί gives the reason: φησιν ὁμοῖον οἷ ἔμεναι is ‘he says that like to himself is’ (οἷ ‘to himself’, ἔμεναι = εἶναι), with οὔ τινα … Δαναῶν οὓς ‘no one of the Danaans whom’. ἔνεικαν is the epic aorist of φέρω.
